title: Building Multi agent Systems with Finite State Machines

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is structuring agents with finite state machines and the Actor model, covering agent loops, planning, multi-agent collaboration, and harness design through five agentic patterns.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is structuring agents with finite state machines and the Actor model, covering agent loops, planning, multi-agent collaboration, and harness design through five agentic patterns.

summary: Adam Terlson argues that finite state machines (FSMs) and the Actor model offer a timeless foundation for building AI agents with predictability, observability, and control—qualities increasingly critical as AI becomes more autonomous. He notes Gartner's 2025 top AI trends are agentic AI (#1) and AI governance platforms (#2), positioning state machines as a potential backbone for governing agent behavior. The talk defines FSMs through a rock-paper-scissors example, covering five components: state definitions, transition logic, guards, actions/effects, and context. State charts extend FSMs with hierarchical and parallel states. The Actor model complements state charts with autonomous entities communicating via message passing, having three capabilities: sending/receiving messages, updating internal state, and creating new actors. State machines define an actor's internal behavior. State machine advantages include predictability, traceability, auditability, recoverability via event log replay, low latency, declarative design, model-based testing, modularity, and the Saga pattern for distributed transactions. Challenges include limited flexibility, state explosion, explicit transition modeling, unmodeled events, concurrency management requiring Azure Service Bus sessions or AWS SQS FIFO message groups, versioning, and a learning curve. Terlson's key insight is that state machine advantages map precisely to LLM weaknesses—LLMs are not predictable, traceable, or recoverable. Combining them leverages each to mitigate the other's limitations. Three building blocks emerge: actors (autonomy and communication), state machines (structure and predictable behavior), and LLMs (dynamic intelligence). Five agentic patterns are introduced in order of increasing autonomy: (1) Tool use—LLM describes how to call tools but does not call them directly; (2) Human-in-the-loop—intermediate authenticated approval steps; (3) Feedback—two agents iterate to improve quality; (4) Collaboration—multiple specialized agents compose into a broader workflow; (5) Orchestration—a centralized LLM planning node determines the next state using event emitters with transition guards; and (6) Chartering—the LLM generates an entirely new state chart, separating planning from execution, demonstrated with o1 creating a data broker opt-out process from a privacyrights.org article. In conclusion, Terlson discusses emergence as a pattern not yet expressible with state charts but argues it will come from making agentic system building feel like composing Legos—specialized units combined into systems greater than the sum of their parts, paralleling React Native, GitHub Actions, and AWS infrastructure as code. He suggests state machines may play a foundational role for the next 70 years. He thanks XState (v5) for powering all visualizations and mentions a 'red versus blue' demo exploring operational aspects with a surprise emergence.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Adam Terlson introduces the talk, framing the challenge of building autonomous AI systems with predictability, observability, and control. He cites Gartner's 2025 AI trends—agentic AI (#1) and AI governance platforms (#2)—and argues state machines may play a foundational role in governing agent decision-making and behavior.

sections.title: What is a Finite State Machine
sections.summary: Defines FSMs as computational models with states and transitions triggered by events, using a rock-paper-scissors example. Covers five components: state definitions, transition logic, guards (enforcing valid transitions), actions/effects (side effects), and context (stored data). Clarifies the distinction between state machines and state charts, noting state charts add hierarchical and parallel states.

sections.title: The Actor Model
sections.summary: Introduces the Actor model as a complement to state charts, providing concurrent, distributed, and encapsulated execution. Actors are autonomous entities with three capabilities: send/receive messages, update internal state, and create new actors. State machines define an actor's internal behavior.

sections.title: Advantages of State Machines
sections.summary: Enumerates state machine advantages: predictability, traceability, auditability, reliability, recoverability via event log replay, time-travel branching, low latency, declarative design, model-based testing, modularity, scalability, and the Saga pattern for distributed transactions with compensating actions.

sections.title: Challenges of State Machines
sections.summary: Covers state machine challenges: limited flexibility, state explosion, explicit transition modeling, unmodeled events, concurrency/parallelism handling (requiring Azure Service Bus sessions or AWS SQS FIFO message groups), versioning difficulties with event log replay, and a learning curve.

sections.title: Complementing LLMs with State Machines
sections.summary: Key insight: state machine advantages are everything LLMs are not. LLMs lack predictability, traceability, auditability, reliability, recoverability, declarative design, and low latency. Combining them leverages strengths of one to mitigate weaknesses of the other. Three building blocks: actors (autonomy/communication), state machines (structure), LLMs (dynamic intelligence).

sections.title: Tool Use and Human in the Loop
sections.summary: Introduces tool use as foundational for agentic patterns. LLM receives tool descriptions, returns how to call them, but does not call methods directly. Human-in-the-loop controls add intermediate authenticated approval steps. Example: recipe writer with inventory retrieval tool (RAG) to constrain output to available ingredients.

sections.title: Feedback and Collaboration
sections.summary: Feedback pattern uses two agents (e.g., recipe writer and nutrition critic) iterating to improve quality. Collaboration extends to multiple specialized agents composing a broader workflow (recipe writer, procurement, preparation, reporting). State machines may lack final states, enabling continuous improvement loops.

sections.title: Orchestration and Chartering
sections.summary: Orchestration lets a centralized LLM planning node determine the next state using event emitters with transition guards. Chartering goes further: the LLM generates an entirely new state chart, separating planning from execution. Demonstrated with o1 creating a data broker opt-out process from a privacyrights.org article, essentially zero-shot.

sections.title: Conclusion: Emergence and Composability
sections.summary: Terlson discusses emergence as a pattern not yet expressible with state charts. He argues that achieving emergence will not come from modeling the human brain but from making agentic system building feel like composing Legos—specialized units combined into systems greater than the sum of their parts, paralleling React Native, GitHub Actions, and AWS infrastructure as code. He suggests state machines may play a foundational role for the next 70 years. He thanks XState (v5) for powering all visualizations, mentions a 'red versus blue' demo exploring operational aspects with a surprise emergence, and invites connection on LinkedIn.
